summary: Registering a GitHub OAuth app is free and self-serve, and you can test it with your own account right away. Organizations with OAuth app access restrictions block their members from using the app until an owner approves it, and that approval depends on the owner, not GitHub.
timeToProduction: Same day for accounts you control. Users in restricted organizations wait for their owner's approval, which GitHub does not control.

gates.title: Any GitHub account can register the app for free
gates.what: You register under your personal account or any organization where you are an admin. No paid plan is needed, and each account or org can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
gates.where: Settings > Developer settings > OAuth Apps, on the account that will own the app. You act here.
gates.todo: Pick the owning account before you register, because the pages do not describe transferring ownership.

gates.title: No test mode was found for OAuth apps
gates.what: The pages describe no sandbox or user cap before launch. Rate limits and token lifetimes apply from day one and are covered under ongoing.
gates.todo: Check the app settings page for any test or unpublished option before you invite testers.

gates.title: No app review was found in the official pages
gates.what: During consent, users see your developer contact information and the list of data the app requests. The pages describe no review queue or verification step for OAuth apps.
gates.where: Nothing to submit was found. Users see the consent screen on GitHub.
gates.todo: Make sure your homepage and contact details are accurate, since users see them at consent.

gates.title: Organizations with access restrictions must approve your app before their data is reachable
gates.what: Members of an organization with OAuth app access restrictions cannot authorize your app for org resources until an owner approves it. New organizations have restrictions on by default, and owners can turn them off.
gates.where: The organization owner acts in the organization's OAuth app access settings. Members request approval from the owner.
gates.todo: Tell users in restricted orgs to request owner approval. Expect some users to be blocked until an owner approves, and do not promise a timeline.

gates.title: No paid API tier was found
gates.what: The pages describe a standard rate limit for authenticated users and no paid tier for API access. Paid plans appear only in GitHub Marketplace listings, which these pages do not cover in detail for OAuth apps.
gates.todo: Confirm in the provider's pricing or API documentation before launch if you need a higher rate limit.

gates.title: Expiring tokens and shared rate limits need ongoing handling
gates.what: Expiring tokens are on by default for new apps, so your app must refresh them. Refresh tokens expire after six months without use, and then users must sign in again. All of a user's apps and tokens share one 5,000 requests per hour limit.
gates.where: Your app's code handles refresh, and the user's own GitHub account holds the shared limit. You act on the code.
gates.todo: Plan a refresh flow and a re-login path for expired refresh tokens. Keep request volume low, since the limit is shared with the user's other tokens.

requirements.text: A GitHub account with admin rights on the personal account or organization that will own the app.
A homepage URL and at least one authorization callback URL, with up to 10 callback URLs allowed.
A GitHub account with a verified email address, which is required before you can authorize any OAuth app.

steps.text: Sign in to GitHub with the account that should own the app, then open Settings > Developer settings > OAuth Apps.
steps.detail: Use the owning personal account or an organization where you are an admin.

steps.text: Enter the application name, the homepage URL, and the authorization callback URL.
steps.detail: Use only public information. Do not put internal URLs in any field.

steps.text: Leave Expire user access tokens checked unless your code does not yet handle refresh tokens.
steps.detail: It is on by default for new apps.

steps.text: Click Register application and copy the client ID.
steps.detail: Keep the client secret server-side only.

steps.text: Check that your authorization requests send a state value, use PKCE with S256, and use a redirect_uri that exactly matches a registered callback.
steps.detail: A redirect_uri that does not match fails.

steps.text: Decide whether your app will use expiring tokens, and plan refresh handling.
steps.detail: Refresh tokens expire after six months without use, and an expired one sends the user back through sign-in.

steps.text: Tell users in organizations with access restrictions to request owner approval.
steps.detail: Owners receive a notification of pending requests. GitHub does not set how long they take.

blockers.problem: Users in an organization see an error or get no org data after authorizing.
blockers.fix: The org has access restrictions on. Users must request owner approval, and the owner must approve the app.

blockers.problem: Authorization fails with a redirect error.
blockers.fix: Register the exact callback URL. With wildcard matching off, the redirect URL must match exactly.

blockers.problem: A user cannot authorize the app at all.
blockers.fix: Verify the email address on the GitHub account first.

blockers.problem: Users are sent back through sign-in after six months.
blockers.fix: The refresh token expired from non-use. Plan a re-login path.

blockers.problem: API calls start failing with rate limit errors.
blockers.fix: Each user's 5,000 requests per hour is shared across all their apps and tokens. Reduce call volume and back off on 403 or 429.

couldNotVerify: The current default for Expire user access tokens in the console. The creating page says enabled, but a 2026 GitHub changelog on token refresh was not read.
Whether the console offers a test or unpublished mode for OAuth apps. None was found in the pages.
Whether any review or verification applies to OAuth apps. The pages describe none, but this is not confirmed.
The settings path for org-owned OAuth apps. A community guide says Organization Settings > Developer settings, but that source is not official.
Whether the console has a separate client secret generation step. The pages mention a client secret but not how to create one.
The June 2026 Help Net Security article is not an official source and was not used for any claim.

claims.statement: You can register an OAuth app under your personal account or under any organization where you have administrative access.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: You can create and register an OAuth app under your personal account or under any organization you have administrative access to.

claims.statement: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.

claims.statement: The OAuth app settings page requires a GitHub login.
claims.note: Probe returned HTTP 200 and redirected to the login page.

claims.statement: You can enter up to 10 callback URLs for an OAuth app.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: You can enter up to 10 callback URLs.

claims.statement: Expiring user access tokens are enabled by default when you create an OAuth app.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: Expire user access tokens is enabled by default.
claims.note: The current creating page says this; a 2026 changelog may differ and was not read.

claims.statement: With expiring tokens, the access token lasts eight hours and the refresh token lasts six months without use.
claims.quote: The access token expires after eight hours, and the refresh token expires after six months without use.

claims.statement: When OAuth app access restrictions are enabled, organization members cannot authorize the app for organization resources.
claims.sourceTitle: About OAuth app access restrictions - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: When OAuth app access restrictions are enabled, organization members and outside collaborators cannot authorize OAuth app access to organization resources.

claims.statement: OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default for newly created organizations.
claims.sourceTitle: About OAuth app access restrictions - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: When you create a new organization, OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default.

claims.statement: Users see the app developer's contact information and the list of requested data when they authorize.
claims.quote: When an OAuth app wants to identify you by your account on GitHub, you'll see a page with the app's developer contact information and a list of the specific data that's being requested.

claims.statement: Requests made with a user's authorization count toward that user's personal limit of 5,000 requests per hour.
claims.sourceTitle: Rate limits for the REST API - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: All of these requests count towards your personal rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour.

claims.statement: With wildcard matching off, the redirect URL must exactly match the registered callback URL.
claims.quote: When wildcard matching is disabled, the redirect URL must exactly match the callback URL.

claims.statement: You must verify your email address before you can authorize an OAuth app.
claims.quote: You must verify your email address before you can authorize an OAuth app.

claims.statement: If a refresh token expires before use, the user must sign in through the web or device flow again.
claims.quote: If your refresh token expires before you use it, you must send the user through the web application flow or device flow again to get a new token pair.

claims.statement: No test mode, app review, or paid API tier for OAuth apps appears in the pages reviewed.
claims.note: Inferred from the absence of any such mention in the pages reviewed; not confirmed in the provider's console.

claims.statement: Hands-on setup takes about 1 hour to register and test, and 2–4 hours in total.
claims.note: Estimate from the number of console steps; the pages give no time.
